story: Erosion has slowly carved Karijini's red landscape out of rock more than 2.5 billion years old. On the plateau, spinifex and snappy gums spread to the horizon; at its edges the ground falls away into gorges about 100 metres deep, their walls stacked with tiers of banded iron formation. From Oxer Lookout you can see four of them, Weano, Red, Joffre and Bilungunha (Hancock), meet above a pool far below. Permanent water is rare in the arid Pilbara, which makes the spring-fed Fortescue Falls, cascading more than 20 metres down natural rock steps into a fern-lined pool, all the more remarkable.

After rain the landscape is covered in yellow-flowering cassias and wattles, northern bluebells and purple mulla-mullas. Large termite mounds dot the grasslands, and the park is home to rock wallabies, echidnas, red kangaroos, goannas, dragons, snakes and many birds. Dingoes are common around the Dales campground. To the west, Punurrunha (Mount Bruce) rises above the Hamersley Range, with views down into the Marandoo iron ore mine just outside the park.

The park is the traditional home of the Banyjima, Kurrama and Innawonga Aboriginal people, and DBCA acknowledges the Banjima, Innawongka and Eastern Guruma people as its Traditional Owners. Karijini is the Banyjima name for the Hamersley Range. Aboriginal land management, such as fire-stick farming, created the mosaic of vegetation types and stages of regrowth that shapes the plants and animals found in the park today. The Karijini Visitor Centre is built in the shape of a goanna moving through country, a symbol for the Banjima people: the tail their history, the head the Traditional Owners' future direction, and Aboriginal Law at the centre.

The area was first protected in 1969, gazetted on 31 October as Dales Gorge National Park; renamed Hamersley Range National Park, it has since taken its Banyjima name. Its gorges carry a reminder of the region's mining past: blue asbestos is present in Yampire and Wittenoom gorges. A park improvement project has upgraded access and facilities, including a sealed road, lookout and toilet at Hamersley Gorge.
howItWorks: Karijini is managed by the Parks and Wildlife Service of Western Australia's Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA), and it is one of more than 30 WA parks with entry fees. The standard fee is per vehicle and covers one day's entry to one or more parks; a WA park pass, from a five-day Holiday Pass to the Annual All Parks Pass, covers park entry everywhere in WA for its duration. Pay entry when you book a campsite, on arrival, or with a pass. Camping fees are separate and are charged per person per night.

There are two places to stay in the park: Dales Campground, run by DBCA, and the Karijini Eco Retreat near Joffre Gorge, which is privately run and also offers glamping and guided tours; an overflow campground opens in peak season. Dales must be booked through Park Stay WA, up to 180 days ahead, and its 153 unpowered sites are in very high demand from June to September. There is no drinking water at Dales; showers are available for a fee at the visitor centre, 12 kilometres away, which is open 9 am to 4 pm and closed from December to February.

The gorge trails are graded, and the hardest, such as Bilungunha (Hancock Gorge) to Kermits Pool and Weano Gorge to Handrail Pool, are Class 5: scrambling, climbing and wading. Do not enter a gorge if rain is about, since flash floods can occur, and leave at once if it starts raining. No dogs or other pets are allowed, campfires are banned at Dales at any time, and DBCA publishes separate rules on drones in Karijini.

sightNotes.poi-au-karijini-fortescue-falls: One of the park's few permanent waterfalls, spring-fed and cascading more than 20 metres down rock steps into a fern-lined pool in Dales Gorge. Swimming allowed.
sightNotes.poi-au-karijini-fern-pool: A lush pool surrounded by paperbarks and delicate ferns near Fortescue Falls, an oasis in a harsh land. Swimming allowed.
sightNotes.poi-au-karijini-ngirribungunha-dales-gor: A challenging two-kilometre return creek-side walk between Fortescue Falls and Three Ways Lookout; the 2.4-kilometre Gorge Rim Walk links Circular Pool and Fortescue Falls lookouts above.
sightNotes.poi-au-karijini-oxer-lookout: From the Weano day-use area, an 800-metre walk to views of the junction of Weano, Red, Joffre and Bilungunha (Hancock) gorges, among WA's most spectacular sights.
sightNotes.poi-au-karijini-handrail-pool: A Class 5 route down Weano Gorge, over boulders, through narrow passages and pools, to a pool reached by handrail. Expect to get wet.
sightNotes.poi-au-karijini-knox-gorge: A 15-minute return walk to Knox Lookout over the meeting of Knox and Wittenoom gorges, or a challenging descent into the gorge itself.
sightNotes.poi-au-karijini-kalamina-gorge: A gentler introduction to Karijini's gorges, with a delightful trail and a picnic area.
sightNotes.poi-au-karijini-hamersley-gorge: In the north-west of the park: swirls of folded rock sweep down the gorge and waterfalls rush into pools. Sealed road to the lower car park, lookout and toilet.
sightNotes.poi-au-karijini-punurrunha-mount-bruce: A Grade 5 nine-kilometre return trail along the ridge, with rocky climbs and views over the Hamersley Range and the Marandoo mine; the Honey Hakea Track is an easier start.

chronology.text: The rock that Karijini's gorges cut through is laid down.
Dales Gorge National Park is gazetted on 31 October; it is later renamed Hamersley Range National Park, today's Karijini National Park.
The Karijini National Park Improvement Project moves on to a new hiking trail along the rim of Red Gorge, its construction out to tender.

safety: Blue asbestos is present in Yampire and Wittenoom gorges; asbestos dust may cause cancer if inhaled. Do not enter them.
Cliff edges are about 100 metres high with loose rock; stay well back. Do not dive or jump into the water.
Flash floods can occur. Do not enter a gorge if there is rain in the area, and leave immediately if it starts raining.
Gorge pools can be extremely cold, especially from April to September; hypothermia can occur. In summer temperatures often pass 40°C: drink plenty of water.
Dingoes around Dales Campground can be aggressive. Never feed them, supervise children, walk in groups and keep food in your vehicle. Carry a personal locator beacon.
regulations: Pay park entry or carry a valid WA park pass.
No campfires at Dales Campground at any time; generators only 8 am to 8 pm in permitted areas.
Carry all rubbish out and use the dump station for portable toilets; no bins are provided.
Stay on marked trails and respect walk classes; Class 5 trails are for fit, experienced walkers only.

weather: Karijini is hot and dry for much of the year. During summer temperatures frequently top 40°C, and November to April is the tropical wet season, bringing storms and the risk of flash floods in the gorges. The busiest time is June to September, when days are milder; but the water in the gorge pools can be extremely cold from April to September, cold enough to cause hypothermia. After rain the plateau fills with wildflowers: cassias and wattles, northern bluebells and mulla-mullas.
directions: Karijini is in the Pilbara region of Western Australia; the nearest town is Tom Price, and the Parks and Wildlife office responsible for the park is in Karratha. A vehicle is essential, both to reach the park and to move between the Dales area and visitor centre in the east, the Weano, Knox and Joffre gorges in the centre and Hamersley Gorge in the north-west, which has sealed road access to its lower car park. Check road conditions with Main Roads WA and DBCA Park Alerts before setting out, and carry plenty of water and fuel.
